proposed_edges.relationship: In “Witch Hunting” (1991), Bartlett criticizes Carlo Ginzburg’s Ecstasies for associating myths across disparate societies without adequate controls and for neglecting their meanings within particular communities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary review read in full on the publisher site. Exact locators: paragraphs beginning “Of course the interpretation of myths” and “Instead of seeking the meanings”, and the concluding discussion beginning “Ginzburg’s poetic intoxication”. Bartlett says “controls are absent” and associations are “entirely subjective”. This records his criticism, not an adjudication; Ginzburg’s book remains unread. See rb_bf_02 for the author’s objections.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Witches’ Sabbath” (1991), Ginzburg challenges Bartlett’s review of Ecstasies for presenting him as asserting actual nocturnal rituals and embracing Jungian psychology, and for omitting his argument about the medieval construction of the sabbath stereotype.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary published letter and Bartlett’s reply read in full. Exact locator: Ginzburg’s four paragraphs under “To the Editors”, especially paragraphs 1–3. He invokes “rituals elude us” and his “explicit rejection of Jung’s approach”. Bartlett disputes these objections in his signed reply. The edge records Ginzburg’s criticism of the review; neither his cited book pages nor the book as a whole was independently read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Jacques Le Goff’s The Birth of Europe in “Off to a Good Start” (2005), Bartlett qualifies its medieval-continuity thesis by stressing industrialization and secularization and criticizing its treatment of Christian oppression.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary review read in full. Exact locators: section 2, paragraphs beginning “Nevertheless, there are fissures” through “We are on one side”, and the final paragraph beginning “Eschewing the Europe”. Bartlett stresses a “great historical divide” and describes Le Goff as “stepping lightly around the long history of Christian oppression”. This appreciative but critical review supplies a bounded disagreement; Le Goff’s book itself remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: John Hudson and William Ian Miller’s “Robert Bartlett: A Profile” (2016) records that Bartlett studied early modern history with Roy Porter at Peterhouse, Cambridge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher preview, printed p. 1, opening paragraph: “he studied the early modern period with Roy Porter”. Authorship and original 2016 publication checked in St Andrews’ institutional record. Influence denotes this documented teaching relationship only; the passage specifies neither a particular methodological debt nor teaching dates. Preview pp. 1–2 read; remaining profile pages and full commemorative volume unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Witch Hunting” (1991), Bartlett presents Keith Thomas’s Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) as a model for explaining witchcraft accusations through social tensions and failures of neighborly charity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Exact locator: review paragraph beginning “A classic example of this approach” and its next paragraph. A named explanatory resource in Bartlett’s argument; no general intellectual allegiance inferred. Thomas’s book remains unread.
